name: Ngorongoro Conservation Area
blurb: Crater lions, hyenas, wildebeest, flamingos and black rhino.

tip.title: Remove the hyenas
tip.text: Spotted hyenas hunt as much as lions in the crater, and lions often take their kills. Lower hyena numbers and watch what happens to lion food and to wildebeest, zebra and flamingos.

notes: The story and why it matters come from the Wikipedia articles listed below (Ngorongoro Conservation Area, Ngorongoro Conservation Area, Spotted hyena). Individual species and links have not been checked one by one. Feeding links that match a GloBI (Global Biotic Interactions) record are marked in the node details, with a link to the records. A few links were added from GloBI records.

nodes.name: Red oat grass
nodes.desc: A tall tussock grass of African grasslands and a recorded food of wildebeest, zebra, buffalo and gazelles in the GloBI database.
A low, spreading grass that carpets grazed ground and is recorded as food for many of the crater grazers.

nodes.name: Umbrella thorn
nodes.desc: A flat-topped thorny tree. Its leaves and pods are browsed by elephants and black rhinos, which prefer acacias.
The most numerous large grazer on the crater floor, though counts have fallen from about 14,700 in 1986 to about 7,250 in the mid-2000s. The most common medium-sized prey of hyenas here.
Grazes alongside wildebeest on the crater floor and in the surrounding plains, and is a regular prey of lions and hyenas.
Numbers have grown in the crater, possibly because fire suppression has favoured tall, fibrous grass. Hyenas largely avoid them, but lions hunt them.
A small grazer of the short-grass plains and crater floor that is hunted by lions, hyenas and jackals.
A browser of leafy plants, twigs and thorny shoots that favours acacias. The crater population fell to 13 in 1993 and had recovered to 55 by 2018.
A huge mixed feeder that eats grass as well as browsing acacia and other trees, opening up woodland.
A small canid that hunts rodents and young antelope and scavenges leftovers from larger carnivores.
A long-legged cat that is widespread in the crater and pounces on rodents in tall grass.
Soars over the plains and feeds on the carcasses of wildebeest, zebra, buffalo and other animals that die or are killed.
The crater holds one of the densest lion populations known, about 62 animals in 2001, but it is inbred and has suffered disease die-offs.
A top predator in the crater. Studies in Ngorongoro found it hunts as much as lions, and lions often take over its kills.
Equatorial sun drives growth of grass, trees and the algae in the shallow lake.
Rains fall in a wet season from about December and draw the large migratory herds on the plains around the crater.
Fertile soils of the old volcano feed the crater grassland.

nodes.name: Dung beetles, fungi & bacteria
nodes.desc: Break down dead plants, dung and carcasses and return nutrients to the soil.

story: Ngorongoro Crater in Tanzania is 610 metres deep, and its floor covers 260 square kilometres. It formed when a volcano collapsed two to three million years ago. The conservation area is part of the Great Migration range of millions of wildebeest, zebras and gazelles.
matters: Fossils at Olduvai Gorge show hominids have lived here for at least 1.75 million years. The Serengeti and Kenya's Maasai Mara share the Great Migration.
